quests.sentence: The woman who called earlier left a message.
quests.ruleExplanation: Who called earlier describes the woman, sitting directly after the noun woman and acting as the subject of its own clause.
quests.nativeTip: Who introduces extra information about a person and sits right after the noun it describes.

quests.sentence: I know the man who fixed our roof.
quests.ruleExplanation: Who fixed our roof follows man directly, identifying exactly which man is being talked about.
quests.nativeTip: The relative clause with who stays right next to the noun it identifies, even inside a longer sentence.

quests.sentence: Employees who arrive late must sign in.
quests.ruleExplanation: Who arrive late follows Employees right at the start, narrowing down exactly which employees the rule applies to.
quests.nativeTip: A relative clause can also follow the subject at the very start of the sentence.

quests.sentence: The laptop which crashed yesterday needs repair.
quests.ruleExplanation: Which crashed yesterday follows laptop, identifying exactly which laptop needs repair — which is used for things, not people.
quests.nativeTip: Which introduces extra information about a thing (not a person), right after the noun.

quests.sentence: She bought a car which uses very little fuel.
quests.ruleExplanation: Which uses very little fuel follows car, describing exactly which kind of car she bought.
quests.nativeTip: The which-clause stays right after the noun, even with a quantity phrase inside it.

quests.sentence: The company launched a product which exceeded expectations.
quests.ruleExplanation: Which exceeded expectations follows product, identifying exactly what kind of product the company launched.
quests.nativeTip: Which still identifies the thing being discussed, sitting right after the noun product.

quests.sentence: The restaurant that opened last month is popular.
quests.ruleExplanation: That opened last month follows restaurant, working the same way which would, since that can replace which in defining clauses.
quests.nativeTip: That can replace which for things in a defining clause, sitting right after the noun.

quests.sentence: The employee that solved the issue got a bonus.
quests.ruleExplanation: That solved the issue follows employee, showing that can replace who for people too, not just which for things.
quests.nativeTip: That can also replace who for people in a defining clause — it works for both.

quests.sentence: The device that stopped working needs new batteries.
quests.ruleExplanation: That stopped working follows device, identifying which device needs new batteries.
quests.nativeTip: That still identifies the specific thing being discussed, right after the noun device.

quests.sentence: The man whose car was stolen filed a report.
quests.ruleExplanation: Whose car was stolen follows man, showing possession: the car belongs to the man, unlike who or that which don't show ownership.
quests.nativeTip: Whose shows possession inside the relative clause — the car belongs to the man.

quests.sentence: She helped the family whose house had burned down.
quests.ruleExplanation: Whose house had burned down follows family, showing the house belongs to that family.
quests.nativeTip: Whose still shows possession, this time linking a family to their house.

quests.sentence: The author whose book won the prize gave a speech.
quests.ruleExplanation: Whose book won the prize follows author, showing the book belongs to that author.
quests.nativeTip: Whose links the author to their book, showing ownership inside the clause.

quests.sentence: This is the restaurant where we had our first date.
quests.ruleExplanation: Where we had our first date follows restaurant, describing the place using where instead of a clunkier phrase like in which.
quests.nativeTip: Where introduces a clause about a place, replacing a phrase like 'in which' or 'at which.'

quests.sentence: The hotel where they stayed was fully booked.
quests.ruleExplanation: Where they stayed follows hotel, identifying exactly which hotel was fully booked.
quests.nativeTip: The where-clause stays right after the place noun, identifying exactly which one is meant.

quests.sentence: I visited the town where my grandmother grew up.
quests.ruleExplanation: Where my grandmother grew up follows town, describing exactly which town is meant.
quests.nativeTip: Where still introduces information about a place, right after the noun town.

quests.sentence: The man who she met became her business partner.
quests.ruleExplanation: Who she met has who as the object of met (she is the one who did the meeting), a different role than the subject who in earlier levels.
quests.nativeTip: Who can also work as the object of its own clause, not just the subject — the person doing the meeting is she, not the man.

quests.sentence: The book which he recommended was fascinating.
quests.ruleExplanation: Which he recommended has which as the object of recommended (he is the one doing the recommending), following the same object-relative pattern.
quests.nativeTip: Which can also be the object of its clause, describing something someone else acted on.

quests.sentence: The car that they bought needs new tires.
quests.ruleExplanation: That they bought has that as the object of bought, describing the car they acted on.
quests.nativeTip: That works as an object relative pronoun too, describing something someone else did something to.

quests.sentence: The book I read was excellent.
quests.ruleExplanation: The book I read drops that/which entirely, since it would be the object of read — this omission is common and natural in everyday English.
quests.nativeTip: When the relative pronoun is the object of its clause, it can often be dropped entirely.

quests.sentence: The people we met were very friendly.
quests.ruleExplanation: The people we met drops who/that, since it would be the object of met, keeping the sentence natural and concise.
quests.nativeTip: The dropped-pronoun pattern works the same way here — no that or who needed.

quests.sentence: The restaurant they recommended is fully booked.
quests.ruleExplanation: The restaurant they recommended drops that/which, since it would be the object of recommended.
quests.nativeTip: The same omission applies here, since the relative pronoun would again be the object.

quests.sentence: My brother, who lives in Canada, is visiting next week.
quests.ruleExplanation: Who lives in Canada sits between two commas because it's extra, non-essential information about my brother — we already know which brother is meant.
quests.nativeTip: Commas surround a non-defining clause on both sides, since it adds extra info rather than identifying which one.

quests.sentence: This restaurant, which opened last year, has become very popular.
quests.ruleExplanation: Which opened last year sits between two commas as extra information about this restaurant; that could not replace which here, since that is never used in non-defining clauses.
quests.nativeTip: The same two-comma pattern surrounds a non-defining which-clause — never that, in this type of clause.

quests.sentence: The engineer, whose company won the award, thanked his team.
quests.ruleExplanation: Whose company won the award sits between two commas as extra, non-essential information about the engineer.
quests.nativeTip: A non-defining whose-clause is also set off by commas on both sides.

quests.sentence: The teacher who taught the class that I loved retired.
quests.ruleExplanation: Who taught the class attaches to teacher, and that I loved attaches to class — two separate relative clauses nested in one sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Two relative clauses can appear in one sentence, each attached to its own noun.

quests.sentence: The hotel where we stayed offered a room that overlooked the ocean.
quests.ruleExplanation: Where we stayed attaches to hotel, and that overlooked the ocean attaches to room — each relative clause identifies a different noun in the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: A where-clause and a that-clause can appear together, each describing a different noun.

quests.sentence: The manager whose team won the award later joined a company that values innovation.
quests.ruleExplanation: Whose team won the award attaches to manager, and that values innovation attaches to company, layering two relative clauses onto two different nouns.
quests.nativeTip: A whose-clause and a that-clause can combine in one long sentence, each modifying a different noun.

quests.sentence: The scientist who discovered the vaccine, which took years to develop, received global recognition.
quests.ruleExplanation: Who discovered the vaccine (defining, no commas) identifies the scientist, while which took years to develop (non-defining, set off by commas) adds extra detail about the vaccine.
quests.nativeTip: Combine a defining who-clause with a non-defining, comma-set-off which-clause in the same sentence.

quests.sentence: The house where they used to live was sold to a family whose children attend the same school.
quests.ruleExplanation: Where they used to live identifies the house, and whose children attend the same school identifies the family — both clauses are defining, with no commas needed.
quests.nativeTip: Combine a defining where-clause with a defining whose-clause, both essential to identifying the nouns.

quests.sentence: The report that she submitted, which impressed the board, led to her promotion.
quests.ruleExplanation: That she submitted (defining, no commas) identifies the report, while which impressed the board (non-defining, set off by commas) adds extra detail about the effect it had.
quests.nativeTip: Combine a defining that-clause with a non-defining, comma-set-off which-clause.
